utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone. Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Stewart, before we ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom, could you give us an estimate on how much time you'd still need.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, certainly. I shall finish comfortably within the first session. As I indicated to Mr. Tieger yesterday, I expected to finish in this session. And at the moment, Your Honour, I expect that I will finish comfortably within one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because we'd like to find some time, at least, to deal with some procedural matters as well. It might be after the first break. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Stewart, perhaps I'm ready to inform you about one of the issues not to be discussed at this moment is the two weeks advanced notice of witnesses and summaries which seems not -- where you earlier talked about always slippage somewhere, that what seems now to be routine rather than slippage somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the matter I would like to discuss at a later stage this afternoon, but perhaps already for you to be aware of what it is. Good afternoon, Ms. Hrvacanin. Before I remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given yesterday, I must admit to the parties that I made a mistake yesterday by not asking the witness not to speak with -- or not asking, but not instructing the witness to speak with anyone about the testimony already given and still to be given. I noticed after the hearing that I had forgotten this. Mrs. Hrvacanin, were you informed by the Victims and Witnesses Section that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Madam Rita told me about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And may I take it that you followed that instruction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I only spoke to my husband, but only about the state of his health.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I apologise for not having instructed you and to the parties as well. But I thought it was better to deal with it in open court so that we also know that Madam Hrvacanin was instructed, although through other channels, not to speak with anyone and that she adhered to those instructions. Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I feel I should have issued a reminder, Your Honour, as well. But if it offers any additional reassurance, I had previously impressed on Ms. Hrvacanin that she should and would be incommunicado during her evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed. Ms. Hrvacanin, as I said before, I remind you that you're still bound by this solemn declaration that you gave yesterday. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Ms. Hrvacanin, you gave evidence yesterday about the frequency of your visits to Sarajevo over various periods and your attendance at the Main Board. I want to ask you about Main Board meetings. When you first were a member of the Main Board from sometime in 1990 onwards, what was a typical number of people who were present at a Main Board meeting when you attended?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first it was between 20 and 25 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And who in the early months when you attended Main Board meetings, if it was indeed the same person, who presided over those meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did that remain the position during the whole of 1990 to 1992, whenever you attended Main Board meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it was all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was Dr. Karadzic always there or were there occasions when, for whatever reason, he wasn't present at Main Board meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was always at Main Board meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was -- were there any other senior figures in the SDS who were either always present or, for practical purposes, nearly always present?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Main Board meetings were usually attended by members of the Main Board. Other people came very seldom, except when necessary. Mrs. Plavsic was not a member of the Main Board, but she often attended Main Board meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were there any other senior figures in the SDS who also often attended Main Board meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understood your question properly. Were -- was there a sufficient member of other senior figures? I mean, if I said that there were members of the Main Board there, I think I've said enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I'm going to, just for the tiny warning to Mr. Tieger, I'm going to risk giving you a batch of names that I'm going to ask you about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: However, Mr. Stewart, it seems to me that perhaps due to a bad translation that the witness had not fully understood the question. Because the way in which she phrases the question when she says that she answered that question already. So could we give it one more try before you do that exercise. Perhaps I would try -- you said at the Main Board meetings, that they were usually attended by members of the Main Board and that other people came very seldom. Were there, among those other people, who, although came seldom, that some people attended, if not frequently then at least with some regularity? Could you name any of the people that came in and attended, apart from Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could I say, with respect, Your Honour, I'm having difficult with the question when it asks: Who among those who came seldom attended, if not frequently at least with some regularly. We seem to have, I believe, a bit of confusion being built in there, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you give us names of other senior SDS people, apart from Mrs. Plavsic, you mentioned already, that would attend meetings of the Main Board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In addition to the members of the Main Board, the members of the Executive Board attended, that is an executive body of the Main Board. Meetings were also attended by some presidents of municipalities when they happened to be there or if they had some questions. Because in essence, Serbs are very inquisitive, they want to know everything, and they also do not trust other people. So often they attended such meetings. The late Vice-President Koljevic also attended meetings. In 1990, I didn't see some other people who were otherwise in political life at meetings of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I -- what I was proposing to do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- and it didn't seem to be a terrible piece of leading, I was proposing to give a list of four, five, six names that would indisputably, I submit, both for the Prosecution and the Defence, be regarded as senior figures in the SDS. We wouldn't say they weren't, the Prosecution say they weren't. I feel relatively confident, Your Honour, that if I give a list of that nature, that's not going to frighten the horses or Mr. Tieger unduly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger is still sitting so I can't see that he objects.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can't speak for the horses, Your Honour, but I'm satisfied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, among senior figures in the SDS who've been discussed in this case, it might be included Mrs. Plavsic, Mr. Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik, Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Dukic, and, of course, Dr. Karadzic, who you've already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't see Mr. Tieger falling apart with fear and consternation of that list.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, among those people, Mrs. Hrvacanin, you've mentioned Dr. Karadzic already, you've mentioned Mr. Koljevic already. Of those other people I've mentioned, did any of them attend with any frequency Main Board meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you mentioned Mr. Velibor Ostojic; he attended all meetings. You mentioned Mr. Dukic, Rajko; he also took part in all meetings. You mentioned Mr. Krajisnik. In 1991 Mr. Krajisnik became a member of the Main Board. Until 1990, he never attended meetings of the Main Board. Well, he wasn't always present at Main Board meetings, but he was present often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, you said a moment ago "that I had mentioned Mr. Krajisnik. In 1991 he became a member of the Main Board." Then you said "until 1990 he never attended meetings of the Main Board." I just ask you: Did Mr. Krajisnik ever attend meetings of the Main Board before he became a member of the board in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I claim that with full responsibility, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So after he became a member of the Main Board, can you remember with what frequency, in percentage terms, of meetings Mr. Krajisnik attended Main Board meetings?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that it wasn't very often, but he did attend sessions of the Main Board. He didn't have any particular influence. He was there. He listened to what other participants in the debate had to say. He hardly ever took the floor at Main Board meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- during the period that you attended Main Board meetings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, before we continue, the witness in the last answer, you, Mrs. Hrvacanin, you said: "No. I said it wasn't very often," whereas the transcript of one of your previous answers reads: "Until 1990 he never attended meetings of the Main Board. Well, he wasn't always present at Main Board meetings but he was present often." Now a few lines later you say: "I said he was -- it wasn't very often," whereas we get a translation of your testimony that he often attended.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that what I said must have been mistranslated. What I said was the following, that Mr. Krajisnik was not a member of the Main Board until 1990, and he never attended Main Board meetings.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: May I pause for a moment. His Honour read back to you an answer where you said "until 1990 he never attended meetings of the Main Board," but I had asked you a supplemental question. Just now -- a moment ago you said Mr. Krajisnik, not a member of the Main Board until 1990. Mrs. Hrvacanin I feel safe in leading here. You have already said, haven't you, and this is correct, Mr. Krajisnik did not become a member of the Main Board until 1991. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can hear some music.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We're all getting music, Your Honour, which is very pleasant in its way but rather disruptive.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not right. It's not right. It doesn't allow me to focus. Your Honour, I did not understand the question put by Mr. Stewart because this music kept coming in and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, relax. I'm sure we shall sort out the music issue for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mrs. Hrvacanin, don't be afraid that anyone puts music on the line in order to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not afraid.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The music is gone now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you repeat your question, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Not to music this time, Mrs. Hrvacanin. It is quite clear, isn't it, Mr. Krajisnik did not become a member of the Main Board until 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And before he became a member of the Main Board, he didn't attend Main Board meetings. Is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what I would now like you to do, Mrs. Hrvacanin, is just to carefully concentrate on informing Their Honours how often, in your recollection, Mr. Krajisnik attended Main Board meetings after he became a member?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: When Mr. Krajisnik became a member of the Main Board, he attended meetings but not often and not regularly. He was president of the Assembly, so when he had time, when he was free, he attended meetings. What the frequency was I cannot say. Was it five times? Was it ten times? I did not go into such analyses, I am sorry, but it was often.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The Main Board meetings that you attended, Mrs. Hrvacanin, what -- what sort of discussions, if you can say this, generally took place in relation to SDS and political matters? What level and type of discussion was there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually it would be a discussion that would start with current issues that had to be resolved. In 1991 the atmosphere was rather heated. The then-Yugoslav army had left Slovenia. Then in Croatia the army was being expelled, too, and we were very upset. When I say "we," I think it was Serbs, Croats, and Muslims who felt upset. Regardless of the fact that I'm an anti-communist, there is still a defence from the point of view of every individual, and that was this army which, regrettably, experienced such a fiasco. At Main Board meetings there were discussions about the Yugoslav national army, which considered us to be enemies. All nationalists, that is, regardless of whether they were Serbs, Croats, or Muslims. So there were such discussions. If anything were to happen, if our former state of Yugoslavia were to fall apart, who would defend us? Since the Main Board had regional representation from all parts of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina, then every member of the Main Board would speak about what was topical for his region or area or town where he lived. Those were mainly the subjects that the Main Board dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the Main Board take decisions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends which decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, is the answer yes or no? It took decisions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It issues recommendations. It could not issue any decisions; it was not in a position to do that. We were a democratic party, which was organised according to a democratic principle. There were no orders and there were no executions of any orders. We would pass conclusions on a certain issue, and those conclusions were binding upon some and not binding upon some others. So, in other words, nobody had to do what the Main Board concluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: To whom or what did the Main Board issue recommendations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the members of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So you're talking about the Main Board issuing recommendations to the members of the Main Board. When you say "it issued recommendations to the members of the Main Board," are you -- do you mean as a group or to individual members?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody received an individual order. An order was not issued to a certain name, but when we arrived at a conclusion, we would agree that something should be done. At that time we were talking about the tripartite, administration in the municipalities, we opted for dialogue, for the establishment of local governments. That was the agreement that we were discussing at the time, so nobody was issued with any orders. It was not a party that was in a position to issue any such orders. Everybody could say whether they wanted to say, and if they didn't do something, it was not punishable in any way for this failure to do things -- or at least I was never punished for not following up on the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, were you ever a member of the Executive Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you ever attend any meeting of the Executive Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. Not once.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you ever invited to a meeting of the Executive Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Would you or did you have any expectation that you should or would be invited to any meeting of the Executive Board of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't expect that. But on one occasion I wanted to attend the meeting of the Main Board, but I was prevented from doing that. At the time the president was Mr. Ostojic, and he said that those who were not members of the Executive Board could not attend any of its meetings. And I accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you able, from your membership of the Main Board and any other activities in connection with the SDS, to form any impression yourself of the relative power and authority of the Main Board and the executive committee?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before the witness answers that question, could I seek clarification from her previous answer. I read your answer translated as it is in English, "but on one occasion I wanted to attend the meeting of the Main Board, but I was prevented from doing that. At the time the time the president was Mr. Ostojic, and he said that those who were not members of the Executive Board could not attend any of its meetings. And I accepted that." Did you want to attend the meeting of the Main Board or of the Executive Board?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Executive Board, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that's either translation or slip of the tongue. Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was very well spotted, if I may say so, Your Honour. I had not noticed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- so what I was asking you then, Mrs. Hrvacanin, was whether you were able to form any impression of the relative power and authority of the Main Board and the executive committee, as between the two of them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Executive Board had more power. In my view the Main Board was nothing but a debate club.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the Main Board ever discuss six strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the Main Board ever discuss Crisis Staffs?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the Main Board ever discuss Variants A and B?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, and I said it already yesterday, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did the Main Board discuss any aspect of any of the international negotiations being conducted in relation to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you present on any occasion at any organ of the SDS when reports were received of the outcome of such international negotiations?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if a member of the Main Board would put a question when people went to The Hague or to Brussels to attend negotiations as to what had happened there, what had been agreed there. If there was such an initiative of one of the members of the Main Board, a report would be submitted in one form or another. But that was a very rare occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, the next point I'm putting to you is not in dispute. There was for a period in the early -- the spring and early summer along to midsummer of 1992, a break in ease of transport and communication between Banja Luka and Pale and a corridor was opened up sometime in late June of 1992. But during that period of a break in ease of communication, did you travel or did you go to Pale at any time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not during that period of time, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you attend the meeting of the Republika Srpska Assembly held in Banja Luka on the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the topics of discussion at that Assembly meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up to then Mrs. Plavsic and Professor Koljevic were elected to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the multi-party elections, and they performed those duties up to that session. At that session, Mr. Radovan Karadzic was proposed as a member of that Presidency. I was informed by the media that Mr. Karadzic had been elected at the president of the Presidency. Mrs. Plavsic and Professor Koljevic were its members, and Dr. Karadzic became its president.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you in 1992 have any knowledge of any organ or group known as the expanded Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you -- in 1992, were you aware of any executive power possessed by Mr. Krajisnik as a -- in whatever capacity as a senior figure in the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik was not a high-ranking member of the SDS. He was a member of the Main Board, as anybody else. He was elected in the multi-parliament -- multi-party elections. He became a deputy and representative of all the three peoples. And later on, he represented only the people of Republika Srpska. He was a member of the Serbian Assembly. He was not a member of the extended Presidency. Such a Presidency did not exist for that matter. There was a Presidency that consisted of three members: Mr. Karadzic, Mrs. Plavsic, and Professor Koljevic. As for some special authorities, Mr. Krajisnik did not have any, save for his own authorities and competences within the work of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Within 1992 and specifically following that meeting of the 12th of May, 1992, in Banja Luka, were you personally aware of anything relating to the six strategic objectives?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was talk about that. I personally don't know anything particular about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Where and between whom did that talk take place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the media. I believe that Cutileiro's plan was discussed by journalists and the six strategic goals. I personally didn't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Within the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would like to ask a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Stewart. It's about an answer that the witness gave us. Speaking about Mr. Krajisnik, she said: He became deputy -- [In English] "And representative of all three peoples, and later on he represented only the people of Republika Srpska." [Interpretation] That's what you said, right? That --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again the interpretation was not good, Your Honour. I said that Mr. Krajisnik was elected as a member of the Serbian Democratic Party during the multi-party elections. But he was appointed into the Bosnian Assembly on behalf of all the three peoples, the Croats, the Serbs, and the Muslims. When the Assembly divided, then it was only the Serbian people, and Serbian representatives joined the SDS group of representatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But in your answer you seem to neglect the fact that he was also president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I wonder whether it might be helped to be specific about which Assembly Your Honour is mentioning at the end of that question in order to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. He was the president of the Assembly of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. So for you, doesn't that mean that he had a more important role than just being an MP representing the people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was the first among the equals. All the representatives stood a chance to be appointed presidents by the way they got into power. The people had chosen them. And Mr. Krajisnik was chosen to be president of the Assembly. He chaired the meetings of the Assembly, but he did not have any particular power. He did not have the power to appoint somebody or remove somebody from any position. He could not issue orders to anybody. Knowing Mr. Krajisnik well, I don't think it's in his nature to do that. He is a great democrat. He is a very tolerant man, and he enjoyed a very charismatic reputation among the people. And during the multi-party elections in Bosnia-Herzegovina, he had been elected by the three peoples there. He was a very good chairman of the Assembly meetings. There were no heated discussions when he chaired the meetings, he didn't prevent anybody from speaking, and that's why he was very popular. But he was not powerful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, regarding Republika Srpska, could you say that he had a certain authority on his colleagues, over his colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but not the highest authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What authority did he have? Could you expand on this a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my previous answer I told you that Mr. Krajisnik did not have a lot of influence, either on the police or on the army, either on any of the ministers or on their appointments or removals, for that matter. His function and his authorities were within the framework of the work that he did, and that was stipulated by the law. I am a doctor. I'm not familiar with the law. I apologise, but this is what I can say because this is as much as I know. His authorities stemmed from the law that provided him with that authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, may I ask the attention, both of you, Mr. Stewart and Mr. Tieger, page 14, lines 12 to 18, the answer starts with: "The election of Mrs. Plavsic and Professor Koljevic to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina." Later on in that answer the words "Presidency" is used again, but I understand this reference to the Presidency not as a reference to the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina anymore but to the Presidency of Republika Srpska, although it's not explicit. If you would understand it in different way, it should be clarified with the witness. If that's your common understanding, then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's my understanding, Your Honour, and I don't see Mr. Tieger --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Yes, Your Honour, may I be clear that Judge Hanoteau finished his --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, he finished, and then I raised --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm obliged, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The -- Mrs. Hrvacanin, at the time of the Banja Luka, Republika Srpska, meeting on the 12th of May, 1992, what -- can you say what degree of either satisfaction or dissatisfaction there was among you and your other active colleagues in the SDS about the formulation of goals for the party?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. At that meeting we did not discuss the goals of the party. Those were a parliamentary Assembly meeting attended by the deputies, if we are referring to the 12th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Mrs. Hrvacanin, I'm really focussing on the date that the -- the time of mid-May 1992. So just to put a date on it and asking you whether at that time, mid-May 1992, whether you can say what level of satisfaction or dissatisfaction there was among active members of the SDS about the formulation of goals of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that Assembly meeting there were no SDS goals. The only thing that happened was the election of President Karadzic. There were no other goals mentioned as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you personally, as a member of the SDS at that time, satisfied that the party's goals were sufficiently clear?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was satisfied. I would not have been a member of that party had I not been satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Just going back to Zenica. You, of course, had left as you told Their Honours. But did you -- in the period as you were leaving and after you left Zenica at the end of February 1992, did you come into any sort of conflict with your former friends and colleagues in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never. I am not fond of conflict. I am that kind of person. I always seek dialogue among people.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any type of disagreement about your activities with anybody in Zenica at that time?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were disagreements. They didn't like me being in the SDS. My colleagues at work told me that I should leave the party. My colleague Alic was a member of the SDA. I was his boss, the head of his service. So I told him: "If you can be a member of your party, why can't I be a member of mine?" And he said: "Of course." I did not enter any particular conflict with anybody. I was not in conflict with anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was any action taken by anybody in Zenica that had a bearing on your own reputation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, that did happen. When I left Zenica, some people did not like the fact that I had saved my hide and that I'm still alive today. There were plans for my assassination. Then they started telling really bad things about me. One of them was that I had given the list of SDS members and of all Serbs to the Muslims, and that based on those lists, the Muslims went on to arrest the Serbs and incarcerate them in the KP Dom Zenica where they were later on ill-treated, starved to death. At one point in time, there were over 300 such people. Mr. Milan Mitrovic wrote a book about that, describing the hardships of Serbs in Central Bosnia. And there was also a serial in Glas Srpski a newspaper published in Banja Luka during the communist times. The name of that paper was only Glas, not Glas Srpski. Well, since I wasn't killed by the Muslims, the Serbs wanted to be the end of me because I had betrayed them. I had a lot of problems with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, first of all, who was it who said that you had given lists of SDS members to the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. This was a story I heard. Mr. Stojan Zivanovic, who is a professor at the school of philosophy in Banja Luka and who is a native of Zenica told me once the war was over -- I was in Zenica and I asked the people whether you had provided the Muslims with some lists. And they said no. And then he said to them: But there are stories to that effect. I don't know who spread those stories, but I know that that story came from Zenica with every refugee that arrived in the territory of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, first of all when you were in Zenica did you in fact have access to lists of SDS members?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not have access to SDS members. This was done by the technical service and the secretary. I never looked at the list of SDS members. I personally believe that this was a private matter of every individual. An affiliation to a party is a private thing. Nobody should know that, and I didn't know who members of the SDS were. I knew about some of my associates, the inner circle of my associates, if they were members of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any truth in any suggestion that you had supplied information about SDS membership in any way to Muslims?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: God forbid. I left suddenly. Nobody knew. The chief administrator of my institution knew because I had told him that I could no longer bear the physical threats. I asked him for an unpaid leave of two months, and then if I could not find a job and a livelihood in Banja Luka, I volunteered to come back to Zenica. He was astonished when he heard that I was leaving. And he said to me: What is the matter with you? You can't leave here. We can protect you. I don't want to lose you as a professional. Unfortunately, I left my husband, stayed there during those two months, and he told me that I should not come back, that I should stay where I was at all costs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions for Mrs. Hrvacanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Perhaps, Mr. Tieger, we are -- I wouldn't say close to the time where we usually have a break since we had a late start. Would you nevertheless prefer to have the break now and then start your cross-examination? Or would you rather start now and have a break to stop in, let's say, approximately 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would prefer the break initially, Your Honour, particularly if we're going to address some procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That seems to make more sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then before we have a break, I have one additional question directly related to questions about SDS membership. Could you tell us how many SDS members there were approximately in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you look at the plebiscite list, you will see that the number was large. There were probably over 2 or 3.000 of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this to say that those who participated in the plebiscite were all SDS members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Over 20.000 people took part in the plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. How could I see on those -- on the plebiscite list, which I think is not in evidence as far as Zenica is concerned -- is it indicated that someone is an SDS member or -- because you say: "If you look at the plebiscite list, you will see that the number is large." I was talking about members of the SDS in Zenica. So how could I read that from that list? Is it indicated, or is there any other way to find out about SDS membership of those who participated in the plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, no. This was not indicated in any way. God forbid that anybody should be marked as an SDS member if they participated in the plebiscite. The Muslims and Croats who wanted to live in a joint state participated in the plebiscite as well, not only Serbs. But when I say that there were over 3.000 of them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you say there were 2 or 3.000, although we cannot learn that from the list. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have those lists. I only have a photo from the founding Assembly of the SDS, and you can tell by the photo that there were over a thousand people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, we have over a thousand and we have 2 to 3.000. I'm just trying to find out how many members there approximately were and what your source of knowledge is. When you mention 2 to 3.000, what was the source of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The source of my knowledge were the local communes with a predominant Serb population such as Raspotocje, Drivusa, Perin Han, and Mutnica. Those people were members of the SDS. In town there were not as many members of the SDS; I'm talking about the centre of town. And if you take into account the number of the population of those local communes, if I do the maths I can tell you that there were about 3.000 SDS members.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you're explaining to me how the membership was spread over the town and some villages. But how would you know that in town there would be less SDS members and in the villages there would be more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because only Muslims lived in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But were all Serbs SDS members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How would you know the number of SDS members? Were they registered somewhere, either in the villages or in the town? I mean if you say "they were not all members," how would you know how many of them were members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was an admission sheet where one was supposed to fill out his name and surname, identification number, date of birth, place of birth, father's name, and the date when this person joined the party or movement, as it was then; and then that went to the headquarters in Sarajevo. Judging by the number of IDs that we got as members of the SDS -- well, every ID had its own number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So membership was registered, was processed through Zenica to Sarajevo, and IDs being sent back. And that's the source of your knowledge of some 2 to 3.000 members of the SDS in Zenica? Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. We will adjourn until 10 minutes -- 5 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber intended to finalise its own discussions on the procedural matters during this break. We couldn't find the time, however, so that is postponed most likely until after the next break. Mr. Tieger, are you ready to cross-examine Mrs. Hrvacanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. In terms of the finalisation of the procedural matters, perhaps I -- I think I understood them to include issues related to the time limits of 65 ter summaries. If not, I could raise that now if they are intended to be raised after the next break, then, of course --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, we'd prefer you to do that after the next break or even tomorrow -- no, we're not sitting tomorrow, I think. But at the earliest occasion. We understood that the Prosecution had quite some concerns about the timing of providing 65 ter summaries, and that's not unnoticed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say that -- perhaps this is what we have in mind now Your Honour's reference to tomorrow. We would have a preference if it -- raised today, simply because I'm going to be here today and I feel I should deal with this matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Preferably, yes. At the same time the Judges need some time to discuss these kind of matters also to form its own preliminary opinion, just perhaps looking at what happened to be certain about what the facts are at this moment before we hear the parties because we could ask specific questions better if we are prepared as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may -- I entirely understand that. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We will try to see whether we could deal with it today. If not, we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, could it be this way, if it's not inconvenient for Your Honour. If it's not possible to be dealt with today, could it be dealt with on Friday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Nothing will change this week, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I feel it's my responsibility to deal with it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If we can't deal with it today you would prefer to deal with it yourself and then preferably on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would simply indicate that Mr. Stewart and I have had a preliminary opportunity to discuss generally the nature of the Prosecution's concerned and its potential impact on the schedule. I simply indicate that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, if Mr. Stewart could take away your concerns or at least diminish them to such a level that you don't have to bother the Chamber with it any more, then, of course, that would be preferred. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I wish that was the case. I was simply --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I try not to aggravate them, Your Honour, that's probably my ambition some of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the level of ambition is not something --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm doing what I can, Your Honour. At least we're talking to each other about it and that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and you're still smiling.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I simply wanted to indicate to Mr. Stewart, that those concerns were going to be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The other matter, by the way, would be the pending admission of exhibits. There are lots of them, some waiting for translation. We would like to categorise them, briefly see what we have, and to make arrangements for solution of this problem so that we -- they would not be pending forever. Also because the Chamber can't proceed if we don't have translations, if we do not know what is in evidence, because, as you'll understood, some digestion of the evidence takes place outside of this courtroom. Then, Madam Usher, could you please escort Mrs. Hrvacanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hrvacanin, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Tieger, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Hrvacanin.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You mentioned, and I believe that's found at page 35 of the LiveNote of the testimony, that's for the benefit of Defence counsel and the Court, that you thought you were in Sarajevo on the 19th, 20th, and 21st of December in connection with the Assembly session you discussed and the meeting that took place in the Holiday Inn that you mentioned thereafter. And I wanted first to ask you whether you were indicating that you were there on all three days or the 19th, 20th, or 21st. Can you tell us what that reference was to, what specific dates you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Sarajevo for three days. I was there on the 19th, the 20th, and the 21st.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And did you customarily arrive in Sarajevo or wherever the site of an Assembly session was a day or two in advance of that session?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could you please speak closer to the microphone, because we can't hear you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think the session was on the 19th -- I beg your pardon, on the 20th. And I came a daily earlier because I had things to do at the dental faculty of the university of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also explained to the Court that you did not know about any similar-size meeting that took place in December of 1991 and did not believe that could have been such a meeting. That was at page 34 -- 44 of the LiveNote, I believe.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying now, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So as far as you're concerned, there was no meeting other than the Assembly session and the spontaneous meeting you testified about of Bosnian Serb officials scheduled for the 19th, 20th, or 21st of December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And by the same token, if there was one that had been scheduled, you don't know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should know if one had been planned, but I don't know anything about a planned meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, this Court has had the opportunity to receive the audio and transcript of a telephone conversation involving Dr. Karadzic on the 19th of December, 1991, in which Dr. Karadzic said, and if --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is, Your Honour, P67 intercept, tab 21. I don't know if it's part of the bundle, but it can be distributed now or later as Court wishes or as counsel wishes. As I say it is in evidence at P67 intercept, tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On that occasion, Mrs. Hrvacanin, Dr. Karadzic said: "They can go fuck themselves. I'll introduce this Friday. I'll introduce a second-degree state of emergency, and I'll teach everyone who fucks around a fucking lesson." And Mr. Novakovic on the other end said: "Is that so?" Dr. Karadzic said: "Yes, yes, they were here from this region and they'll let you know who needs to come. It's our Assembly session here on Saturday." For your benefit, Mrs. Hrvacanin, having checked the calendar for 1991, I can tell you the 21st of December was a Saturday, the 20th was a Friday. Then Dr. Karadzic continued in the conversation at a slightly later point after saying, as Mr. Novakovic said: "So we'll be here on Saturday. Is that right?" And Dr. Karadzic said: "On Saturday -- and on Friday all these people of yours need to come. You have it there about how -- who needs to come and so" -- and Mr. Novakovic asks: "Uh-huh, all right, all right. What does this second degree imply?" Dr. Karadzic says: "Well, you'll see." I take it from you've told us earlier then, you don't know anything about any meeting on Friday or on the day before the scheduled Assembly session during which Dr. Karadzic would introduce this state of emergency?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, that I didn't know anything about this. But by your leave, Your Honours, there is something strange about this. Dr. Karadzic does not swear at all when he speaks, whereas many swear words were used in this passage. I don't want to express any doubts or suspicions, but perhaps the interpreters have misinterpreted this because this is very bad behaviour, all this swearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Hrvacanin, I fully agree with you that swearing is not what one would expect from civilised persons, but the Chamber is in a position, in view of the many intercepts we have listened to, to form its opinion on whether swearing of -- by the person identified in these telephone conversations as Mr. Karadzic, whether that is exceptional or not. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In addition, Mrs. Hrvacanin, the diary kept by Dr. Karadzic, chef de cabinet, reflects a notation by what appears to be a meeting of the Main Board at 1600 on December 20th, 1991, and, again, which is Friday. There are two notations on that date. In the calendar, 1600 meeting of Main Board, and 1600 Main Board on the page below.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is, for the Court's benefit, P893, I think tab 2 -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, that's incorrect. It is P65 Treanor 5, tab 65, and P529, Hanson tab 374.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Again, Mrs. Hrvacanin, I take it from what you've told us earlier that you don't know anything about this reference to a Main Board gathering at 1600 on December 20th, 1991, the day before the Assembly session was held?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly. I don't know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday you were shown the document that is -- has been called Variant A and B, the instructions of December 1991 and indicated you had never seen that. When you were in -- well, in Sarajevo the 19th, 20th, and 21st, did Dr. Karadzic or Mr. Krajisnik issue anything requiring implementation?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember - and that's what I said yesterday - no. Neither Dr. Karadzic nor Mr. Krajisnik were distributing any kind of material at that session. Now, whether somebody else was, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now directing the Court's attention to P529 Hanson tab 383.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, Mrs. Hrvacanin, when Dr. Karadzic said to Mr. Krajisnik in a telephone conversation of 21 December 1991: "You know what, who will implement what we issued last night?" You don't have any idea what he's referring to, do you, according to you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you told the Court that you wanted to attend the session that took place, the Assembly session that took place in late December because there were some items on the agenda that you felt were important. And you said: "What the coat of arms would be and what the anthem would be in the republic."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Were those items or issues important enough to you so that you spoke at the Assembly about them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll turn to that in a moment, but I wanted first to discuss with you the reason you gave for the proposal to have a spontaneous meeting after the Assembly ended at approximately 12.00, as you told us. And I believe you explained that the delegates wanted to discuss the memorandum regarding independence and didn't want to do so in the blue hall for fear of being overheard. I think you in fact mentioned that Serbs had loud voices. Is that essentially correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So I take it then that there was a reluctance to discuss it before the group had adjourned to the Holiday Inn, and the group members, the Assembly members, refrained from doing so until they had safely gathered at the Holiday Inn for the spontaneous meeting. Is that essentially right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Apart from the issues of emblems and anthems, do you recall what was discussed at the Assembly session that took place, according to you, on or about December 20th, 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that most of it focussed on the coat of arms and the anthem. And I also think that independent MPs joined the Serb Assembly, but please do allow for the possibility that I do not remember everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I do indeed, ma'am. Well, I'm sure it won't surprise you to learn that records were kept of the Assembly sessions, and I've had an opportunity to look at the record of the Assembly session that was held on December 21st, Saturday, 1991. And the first item on the agenda, Mrs. Hrvacanin, was in fact the declaration on the guidelines for recognition of new states by the council of ministers of the European Community. And three speakers spoke about that right away: First, Mr. Buha at page 3. He complained about this declaration by the European community, and in doing so referred to the illegal memorandum and platform adopted against the will of the Serbian people. Then Mr. Koljevic spoke. He referred to a text that was submitted to the Presidency of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which stated flatly: Opposition to Bosnia and Herzegovina submitting an application for independence to the European Community. And then Mr. Simovic spoke, and he indicated that the position of the Bosnian Serb authorities was expressed in a statement entitled "Black Friday for Bosnia and Herzegovina." And again he made the position of the Bosnian Serb authorities on the memorandum for independence and on the movement towards independence, quite clear, describing it as it was described in the statement as a flagrant violation of the constitution. And then the Assembly prepared, in fact, a letter to Lord Carrington referring to the "brutal violation of the constitutional system by the adoption of the Bosnian authorities of the memorandum and the subsequent request for recognition." Now, does that at all refresh your recollection that the position of the Bosnian Serb authorities and all the delegates there was quite explicit and quite clear, and there was no -- there was no need for a subsequent meeting to thrash out in any way or to identify secretly in any way the position regarding the memorandum?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recall what you just said, Mr. Prosecutor. I have no reason to doubt it. I believe that all of it is true, but my memory doesn't serve me very well now. I know for sure that it was said that we should go to the Holiday Inn and have lunch there and, if necessary, we'll talk over lunch. I stand by the statement I made yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps in light of what I've just read to you, it wasn't necessary to discuss the position on the memorandum but maybe some other matters. So let me ask you first whether you recall any discussion at the Assembly session about what the Bosnian Serbs would do in response to their opposition to the memorandum and to the effort by the Bosnian government to seek independence?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if I may, let me indicate a few speakers at that session and what they said. First of all, do you recall anyone saying: "Unless the Muslims and Croats change their minds, this will be known as the beginning of the rebellion against the tyrants"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Dukic said that at page 19 of the English transcript. Do you recall anyone saying that: "It is a lie that it is possible to live together"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was Mr. -- Dr. Koljevic of page 44 of the English transcript. Do you recall anyone saying that: "The aim should be as much separation as possible"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic at page 41. What about someone saying: "Each party should take what is theirs, and for Serbs that means the areas where they are a minority because of World War II or because of colonisation or because people move to Serbia"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Zekic at page 18.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The deputy who was killed, Mr. Zekic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct. Do you recall anyone saying that: "There will be new borders"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was Mr. Miskjen [phoen]. Mrs. Hrvacanin, do you recall someone saying that: "If the European community goes ahead with the threat to recognise Bosnia and Herzegovina as independent state, there will be another Serb uprising and massive bloodshed in which some nations that have been subsequently created will disappear"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was Dr. Vukic who said that, and his reference to "nations that had been subsequently created," you understand as a reference, I presume, to the fact that the Muslims did not become a "narod," a nation until 1974?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were a narod, a people, but they were recognised as a nation in 1974, but they were there as a people, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. But that's how you understand that reference, I take it. Is that right? I see you nodding your head "yes." Thank you. And do you recall anyone saying that: "The alternative to acceptance of the Serb proposals is civil war" and that that "civil war would involve massive deaths and destruction and massive population movements and population homogenisation"? Do you recall that, Mrs. Hrvacanin?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was Dr. Karadzic at page 40. In any event, after discussing all of this at the Assembly session, according to you the assembled representatives decided that there was a need for some more secure place to continue the discussion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, after discussing the opposition to the memorandum and after discussing the response and proposed response to the memorandum and the attempt by the Bosnian authorities to seek sovereignty and independence, was there anything left for the gathered representatives to discuss, other than how to prepare to do these things, that is to create new borders, to homogenise the population, and to make the Muslims disappear, as Dr. Vukic had said and as Dr. Karadzic referred to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a very ugly thing even to hear something like that, that somebody should disappear. I think that the aspiration of the Serb people was to live in Yugoslavia. That was a recognised state of all nations, Muslims, Croats, Serbs, Montenegrins, all of those who lived there. I never heard of any such idea or any such story, that the Serbs should make a border of their own, except that Bosnia and Herzegovina should be within the framework of Yugoslavia. That is why the Serbs asked for the plebiscite, not like the referendum of the Muslims and the Croats to recognise independence. I think that that is the only example of something like this happening through a referendum, so I'm not aware of this, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the way, Mrs. Hrvacanin, I also recall that you said during your testimony when you were being questioned by Mr. Stewart that Dr. Karadzic was not at the Assembly session in -- that you described, in December of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct that I said that. I don't remember that he was there, but then you say he was there. I don't remember though.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact Dr. Karadzic spoke four times at some length from pages 19 to 21, from pages 37 to 42, again at page 48 and 49 of an English transcription of the session which was a total of 50 pages. Let me ask you some more questions, if I may, about what you've told us about that session. First of all, you said that the Assembly meeting you attended on December 19th, 20th, or 21st, which I think you identified today as being on the 20th, went from around 10.00 onwards. That's at page 37 of the LiveNote. I'm actually quoting: "From around 10.00 onwards." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's right. I think that's what I said. It's been 13 years. Allow for the possibility that I may not remember some things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you said that it: "Took place in the so-called blue hall of the municipality building." Correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Assembly, yes. I think that is what it was called because the chairs were blue, that the general decor was in blue hues, so I think that's the name of the room, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mrs. Hrvacanin, the records of the Assembly session held on December 21st, 1991, reflect that it did not begin at 10.00 but it began at shortly after noon, at about 12.16, and then continued on into the afternoon. And the records further reveal that it was not held in the blue hall or blue room, but in the Holiday Inn hotel. And the record further indicates, Mrs. Hrvacanin, that anthems and coats of arms or emblems were neither on the agenda of the meeting 21 December nor discussed. You're welcome to see the records of that, but if you accept that, we can move forward.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no reason not to believe you, but I don't know of Assembly meetings being held at all at the Holiday Inn.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, in fact, Mrs. Hrvacanin there was an Assembly meeting that was held at the Holiday Inn, at least one that I'm about to describe -- oh, I'm sorry, pardon me. Let me rephrase that. I actually want to turn your attention to a meeting at which, contrary to the meeting of 21 December, anthems and coats of arms were in fact discussed, as you described, and at which you spoke about anthems and coats of arms. And further --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- which began around 10.00, as you describe about the meeting, and which was held in the blue hall, as you described. But, Mrs. Hrvacanin, that was not the meeting of 21 December, not the Assembly session of 21 December, 1991; that was the Assembly session held on 15 February 1992, the seventh session of the Assembly. So, Mrs. Hrvacanin, in light of all that, do you agree that the meeting -- the Assembly session you were talking about was not held in December, December 20th or December 21st, as the record in fact indicates, but was held in mid-February 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Now that you've said it in this hall, in this room, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And any spontaneous meeting that took place after the session that you've described at which no documents were distributed would have taken place in the afternoon of February 15th, 1992? That follows logically, I take it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As long as we're on the subject of Assembly sessions, perhaps this is a good opportunity to ask you a few questions about the Assembly session on the 12th of May, 1992, in Banja Luka. That's the session that you were asked about earlier this afternoon. And I think you told the Court that what you remembered about that particular Assembly session was that Dr. Karadzic became a member of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Stewart asked you a few questions about the six strategic objectives or goals, and you said that although there was -- essentially, although there was talk about it in the media, that you didn't know anything about it and had never heard anything directly about the six strategic objectives or goals?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And then he subsequently asked some questions about goals discussed at the Assembly session of 12 May 1992, and again you said the only thing that happened was the election of Dr. Karadzic. And you said: "There were no other goals mentioned, as far as I know."

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I attended those sessions, but I wasn't there all the time. I would sometimes leave the room. However, this doesn't justify me not knowing what happened at those sessions. Still, I can tell you what I really remember and what I told you is the truth. And if I don't remember something, then obviously I can't talk about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So are you now saying that you're not sure what was discussed at that session or that you're sure that nothing significant, other than Dr. Karadzic's becoming a member of the Presidency, happened at that session and particularly no discussion of strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you said is certain. Mr. Karadzic was appointed president. First he became a member of the Presidency and then president. This was very important because he was also the leader of the party. As for the strategic goals, I don't know anything about those. If this -- whether this was important, whether this was at all discussed, I don't know. And I'm telling you the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, as you pointed out, it certainly happens that people step away from a meeting for a short time for a bathroom break or for a cup of coffee, and I guess everyone understands that. But at this particular meeting, Mrs. Hrvacanin, the strategic goals were discussed or mentioned, I believe, a total of ten times. And let me describe those quickly for you. First of all, Dr. Karadzic described the six strategic objectives. That's found at pages 13 and 14 of the English translation. Then Mr. Kerovic at page 17 said: "I would only like to add in relation to the strategic goals presented by Dr. Karadzic," and then continued. Then Mr. Milosevic referred to the second strategic goal and discussed the work that should be done on that, page 18. And then Mr. Djuric began by says: "Mr. President, fellow deputies, I would like to say a word on these strategic goals." Then Mr. Vjestica said: "I would like to accept all the goals that have been proposed." Then Mr. Novakovic said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, I ask you also, if you have it available, the pages so that the Judges can form an opinion whether it was ten times referred to in five or ten pages, or more spread over the whole meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course. I don't know where I left off. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You stopped with Mr. Djuric. That's the first time when you didn't give a page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Djuric at page 20, Mr. Vjestica at page 24, then Mr. Novakovic at page 25 and 26 discussed the work that had been done with maps he said: "Not because the Serbs like to draw maps, although it is true that they do, but because our strategic goals, or rather concrete tasks for all the deputies here and all the people's tribunes, military leaders and others on the ground should be derived from such an explanation." Then Mr. Ostojic at page 31 said -- it was an appeal to start working and said: "The third thing as far as realisation of strategic goals is concerned." And then he talked about a further development of the goals and variations on the goals and sub-goals. Mr. Mijatovic at pages 35 through 36 said: "I would like to say the following concerning the realisation of all the six strategic goals that are the duty for all of us of the Serbian republic." Then General Mladic at page 36 said: "To achieve a goal, you need forces. I have read and mulled over for a long time and discussed within the most select circle of comrades who we convened the strategic goals that are of substance." Then Mr. Krajisnik at page 49 said: "Strategic goals, please, I would like to offer an explanation." And he began discussing the corridor mentioned between Krajina and Semberija. "The size of the corridor depends on you," he said. And then he continued as he went on: "As for the goals, I would just like to offer an explanation since I have also taken part in adopting these goals."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, in light of all that, can we accept that your failure to recall any reference to the strategic goals at that session is not a function of stepping out briefly for a cup of coffee or to the bathroom, but for some other reason such as a failure of memory or blocking it out or whatever reason you may offer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason must be that I have suppressed a lot of things that happened to me in Zenica and later on. I don't know if the strategic goal was to separate the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the people in it from the Serbs. At least this is what I learned from the media. The corridor had not existed. You could see in my CV that I was born in Belgrade. I couldn't go to Belgrade because there was no corridor. Whether this corridor could have been created in one way or another, I can't tell you because I'm not an expert. But I know for a fact that General Mladic attended that session and all the gentlemen that you have mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't find that important, and that is why I didn't pay too much attention, I didn't listen carefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, could we ask the witness to explain the first line of her previous answer. You said: "The reason must be" - when you were asked about your failure of memory - "that I have suppressed a lot of things that happened to me in Zenica and later on." That's not entirely clear to the Chamber. Could you explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I experienced a lot of trauma in Zenica and later on as well. I underwent treatment. I had nocturnal urination and various kinds of stresses, and that's why I'm saying that I don't want to remember some things. I was 45 at the time - now I'm 60 - and I still suffer consequences. Nothing else that I can add to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say "I underwent treatment," could you tell us something about the type of treatment. Could be -- and if you would feel uncomfortable in telling these private matters, very private matters, in open session, then we could consider, if you would ask us to do so, to go into private session for a moment and to hear from you. It could be -- I mean medical treatment, could be by someone -- there are a lot of disciplines in medicine. So I'm not inviting you, but if you prefer to do that please let us know. And could you please answer my question on what type of treatment you underwent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We don't need to go into private session for this. I still depend on drugs. I suffer from cardiac and vascular diseases. I suffer from hypertension. I also have angina pectoris. I have chronical pancreas disease. Those are the illnesses that are aggravated by certain situations. I still take a lot of medicines. I am under a constant medical supervision, and the illness that I suffer from is progressing. And it got worse -- it got worse during the period when I was stressed out in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mentioned quite some medical problems. Did the treatment -- because at the very end you say: "The illness I suffer from is progressing." You mentioned quite a number of illnesses. Were you treated by -- or did you consult psychiatrists and psychologists as well in this respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there's no need for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No, I just wanted to be sure. And do you take any tranquillisers or psychopharmica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mrs. Hrvacanin, I noticed in your answer that you said: "I don't know whether -- I don't know if the strategic goal was to separate the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina or the people in it from the Serbs." Your 65 ter summary indicates that you were friendly with and spoke frequently, among other people, Vojo Kupresanin. Do I understand that correctly?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you knew Mr. Kupresanin to be someone who was a regional leader and had the opportunity to interact on a reasonably regular basis with republic-level leaders. Is that basically correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Did you have any doubt that Mr. Kupresanin was someone who understood the strategic goals?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He would have been somebody you would have expected to be aware of them and understand them, however; isn't he?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Kupresanin is a high school graduate. He is a teacher by profession.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But it's not very difficult, I think, to understand the difference between separating a country and separating the people in the country from the other people in the country; right? That's pretty fundamental. You don't need to go to college to understand the difference, do you?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODANKA HRVACANIN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, but this is a very lofty question that you ask me. If the desire was for us to live in Yugoslavia, then I really don't know who we were supposed to separate from.
